newsitem.title: USA: Strawberry scare fuels US food safety agency push.
newsitem.headline: Strawberry scare fuels US food safety agency push.

text.p: Last week's outbreak of hepatitis-A among Michigan schoolchildren has provided ammunition to consumer groups seeking a major overhaul of the nation's food inspection system.

With foodborne illnesses on the rise, they argue the best remedy would be to create a single agency dedicated to food safety. Currently the Food and Drug Administration, the Agriculture Department and the Environmental Protection Agency share responsibility for monitoring the nation's food supply.

More than 170 Michigan schoolchildren and teachers got sick last week after eating tainted frozen strawberries in government school lunch programme desserts. Thousands of children across four states received hepatitis innoculations after eating the suspect berries, which were grown in Mexico.

The scare was the latest in a tide of foodborne illnesses including E.coli 0157:H7 poisoning traced to lettuce and unpasteurized apple juice that made some 200 people sick and killed one child in 1996, and Vibrio vulnificus in Gulf Coast oysters, which claims dozens of lives each year.

"We have a lot of emerging problems in the food supply. New parasites, new bacteria. Things are showing up in unexpected places," said Caroline Smith DeWaal, director of food safety at the Centre for Science in the Public Interest.

"Our system of food inspection is outmoded," Carol Tucker Foreman, who heads a coalition of labour unions and consumer groups, said. "There is no reason for continuing the division created back at the turn of the century when the first meat inspection act and the first food and drug act passed."

Consumer groups say years of agency underfunding have accompanied mounting problems. Not only do the FDA and USDA food agencies face the challenges of deadly new bacterial foes such as E. coli 0157:H7, which was first discovered in 1982, but they must grapple with changing consumer habits.
As Americans dine out more they become more susceptible to foodborne illness. And an explosion of imports of fresh fruit, vegetables and meat has put pressure on the system.
A government audit found the Agriculture Department has been unable to keep up with its inspections of the big influx of fresh produce coming in from Mexico as a result of the NAFTA trade agreement.

Foodborne illnesses make some 33 million people sick each year in the United States and kill 9,000. Health officials say the numbers are rising but part of that may be due to improved surveillance and a better understanding of bacteria.

Thomas Billy, administrator of the Agriculture Department's Food Safety and Inspection Service, cited the recent overhaul of meat inspection and President Clinton's proposal to spend $43 million to track foodborne illnesses more aggressively.

He said he would "be very concerned that an effort right now in terms of making another substantial change along the lines of moving to a single food agency would disrupt the important changes under way."
